enc.title: Lecture questions: lattices and crystal structures

source.where: Week 1 (chapters 1.1–1.2): the concept questions asked in the lecture, with the answers marked on the slides

questions.q: Yes or no? All unit cells possess exactly 1 lattice site.
questions.explain: Only primitive unit cells do. Conventional cells are often larger: the BCC cube holds 2 lattice points, the FCC cube 4 (script 1.2.1, Fig. 1.2).

source.where: slide 16; no key on the slide, the answer is ours

questions.q: Yes or no? There are infinitely many primitive unit cells.
questions.explain: Any cell that tiles space under the lattice translations and contains one lattice point is primitive: you can shear the parallelogram as you like (Fig. 1.2), and the Wigner–Seitz cell is one more.

source.where: slide 16; no key on the slide, the answer is ours

questions.q: Yes or no? All primitive unit cells have the same volume.
questions.explain: Each holds exactly one lattice point, so its volume is (total volume)/(number of lattice points) $=|\mathbf a\cdot(\mathbf b\times\mathbf c)|$, whatever its shape.

source.where: slide 16; no key on the slide, the answer is ours

questions.q: Yes or no? All Bravais lattices are also unit cells.
questions.explain: The cell drawn for each Bravais lattice (cube, centred cube, hexagonal prism ...) tiles space under lattice translations, so it is a unit cell: the conventional one, chosen to show the symmetry.

source.where: slide 16; no key on the slide, the answer is ours

questions.q: Yes or no? All Bravais lattices are also primitive unit cells.
questions.explain: The centred ones are not: body-centred, face-centred and base-centred conventional cells contain 2, 4 and 2 lattice points. Their primitive cells are smaller and hide the cubic symmetry.

source.where: slide 16; no key on the slide, the answer is ours

questions.q: Yes or no? All 2D lattices can be assigned to one of the 5 Bravais lattices.
questions.explain: In 2D there are exactly five: oblique, rectangular, centred rectangular, square, hexagonal (14 in 3D, script 1.2.3). Every lattice falls into one of them by its symmetry.

source.where: slide 16; no key on the slide, the answer is ours

questions.q: Which structure is shown?
questions.explain: Hexagonal layers stacked A B A: a hexagonal lattice with a two-atom basis. The three atoms in the middle plane sit over every second triangle of the layer below. HCP is not a Bravais lattice.

source.where: slide 33; the slide marks this answer

questions.q: Which structure is shown?
questions.explain: Two FCC lattices shifted by $(\frac14,\frac14,\frac14)$ along the space diagonal, every atom with four tetrahedral neighbours. Two different atoms: zincblende (ZnS, GaAs). With identical atoms it would be diamond (Si, Ge).

source.where: slide 34; the slide marks this answer

questions.q: Which structure is shown?
questions.explain: Corners plus face centres: face-centred cubic, 4 atoms per cube, 12 nearest neighbours at $a/\sqrt2$.

source.where: slide 35; the slide marks this answer

questions.q: Which structure has the atomic layering shown?
questions.explain: Close-packed layers in the sequence A B C A B C are FCC (the layers are its $(111)$ planes). A B A B is HCP. Both fill 74% of space.

source.where: slide 36; the slide marks this answer

questions.q: Which two-atomic lattice has the highest packing density?
options: It depends on the ionic radii
questions.explain: With two kinds of spheres the densest arrangement depends on the ratio of the radii: which structure lets anions and cations touch without the anions overlapping (CsCl for similar radii, NaCl for a smaller cation, ZnS for a much smaller one).

source.where: slide 37; the slide marks this answer

questions.q: What is the coordination number of an HCP lattice?
questions.explain: 6 neighbours in the own close-packed layer, 3 above and 3 below: 12, the same as FCC. That is the maximum for equal spheres.

source.where: slide 38; the slide marks this answer

questions.q: What is the number of atoms per (conventional) unit cell in a BCC lattice?
questions.explain: $8\times\frac18$ from the corners plus 1 in the centre: 2. The primitive cell therefore has volume $a^3/2$ (sheet 2 Q1).

source.where: slide 39; the slide marks this answer
Week 2 and the week-8 quiz (chapter 1.3): the concept questions asked in the lecture, with the answers marked on the slides

questions.q: Which reciprocal lattice belongs to the direct lattice shown?
questions.explain: $\mathbf a^*\perp\mathbf b$ and $\mathbf b^*\perp\mathbf a$ (script eq. 1.8: $\mathbf a^*\cdot\mathbf b=0$). $\mathbf a$ is horizontal, so $\mathbf b^*$ must be vertical; $\mathbf b$ leans to the left, so $\mathbf a^*$ is tilted upwards. Only panel 2 has both.

source.where: slide 51; the slide marks this answer

questions.q: Which reciprocal lattice belongs to the direct lattice shown (a and b enclose 120°)?
questions.explain: The reciprocal of a hexagonal lattice is hexagonal again, rotated by 30°. With 120° between $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf b$, the vectors $\mathbf a^*\perp\mathbf b$ and $\mathbf b^*\perp\mathbf a$ enclose 60°.

source.where: slide 52; the slide marks this answer

questions.q: What is the Miller index of the lattice plane?
questions.explain: The plane contains the origin and the points $(\frac12,1,0)$ and $(0,1,\frac12)$, so its normal $(h,k,l)$ obeys $\frac h2+k=0$ and $k+\frac l2=0$: $(hkl)\propto(2,-1,2)$. Check with the neighbouring plane of the family, $2x-y+2z=1$: intercepts $\frac12$, $-1$, $\frac12$, reciprocals $2,-1,2$. A plane through the origin has no intercepts: always shift to a parallel one.

source.where: slide 53; the slide marks this answer

questions.q: A hexagonal lattice in direct space with $a_1=a_2=1$ Å. What is the volume (area) of the first Brillouin zone?
questions.explain: Every primitive cell of the reciprocal lattice has the area $(2\pi)^2/A_{\rm cell}$ (sheet 1 Q3c in 2D). $A_{\rm cell}=a^2\sin60^\circ=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}$ Å$^2$, so $A_{BZ}=\frac{4\pi^2}{\sqrt3/2}=\frac{8\pi^2}{\sqrt3}$ Å$^{-2}$. Units: inverse area.

source.where: slide 2; the slide marks this answer

questions.q: A two-dimensional lattice with rotational symmetry and a single lattice constant $a$. Which statement is correct?
options: The two reciprocal lattice vectors do not necessarily have the same length
The volume of the first Brillouin zone is $1/a^2$
To compute the structure factor, only atoms closer than $a$ need to be considered
The angle between the basis vectors is 60°, 90° or 120°
questions.explain: One lattice constant plus a rotation axis means square (90°) or hexagonal (60° or 120°, the same lattice). Then $|\mathbf a^*|=|\mathbf b^*|$; the zone area is $(2\pi)^2/A_{\rm cell}$, not $1/a^2$; and the structure factor sums over all atoms of the basis in one cell.

source.where: slide 4; the slide marks this answer

questions.q: A lattice with the unit vectors $(a,0,0)$, $(0,a,0)$ and $(\frac a2,\frac a2,\frac a2)$. Which statement is correct?
options: The reciprocal lattice vectors are orthogonal
The unit vectors describe a two-atomic basis
The lattice is a body-centred cubic (BCC) Bravais lattice
Each lattice site is occupied by one atom
questions.explain: $2\mathbf a_3-\mathbf a_1-\mathbf a_2=(0,0,a)$: the vectors generate all cube corners and, with $\mathbf a_3$, all body centres: BCC. Lattice vectors say nothing about the basis or how many atoms sit on a site, and the reciprocal vectors (an FCC set) are not orthogonal.

source.where: slide 8; the slide marks this answer

questions.q: Given an FCC direct lattice, what is its reciprocal lattice?
questions.explain: FCC and BCC are reciprocal to each other (sheet 2 Q1): FCC with cube edge $a$ gives BCC with cube edge $4\pi/a$. Its first Brillouin zone is the truncated octahedron.

source.where: slide 11; the slide marks this answer

questions.q: Given a BCC direct lattice, what is its reciprocal lattice?
questions.explain: $\mathbf b_1=\frac{2\pi}{a}(\hat{\mathbf y}+\hat{\mathbf z})$ and cyclic: an FCC lattice with cube edge $4\pi/a$ (sheet 2 Q1). First Brillouin zone: rhombic dodecahedron.

source.where: slide 12; the slide marks this answer

questions.q: Given a SC direct lattice, what is its reciprocal lattice?
questions.explain: Orthogonal vectors of equal length stay orthogonal and equal: simple cubic with lattice constant $2\pi/a$. The first Brillouin zone is a cube.

source.where: slide 13; the slide marks this answer

questions.q: Given a hexagonal direct lattice, what is its reciprocal lattice?
questions.explain: Hexagonal again, rotated by 30° about the $c$ axis, with in-plane constant $\frac{4\pi}{\sqrt3a}$ and $2\pi/c$ along the axis.

source.where: slide 14; the slide marks this answer

questions.q: An FCC lattice with cube edge $a_0$. What is the volume of the primitive unit cell?
questions.explain: The cube contains $8\times\frac18+6\times\frac12=4$ lattice points, and a primitive cell contains one: $a_0^3/4$.

source.where: slide 16; the slide marks this answer
Week 2 and the week-8 quiz (chapter 1.5): the concept questions asked in the lecture, with the answers marked on the slides

questions.q: Yes or no? $\lambda=2d_{hkl}\sin\theta$. The Bragg condition can be fulfilled for any wavelength $\lambda$.
questions.explain: $\sin\theta\le1$ requires $\lambda\le2d_{hkl}$. For $\lambda$ larger than twice the largest plane spacing there is no Bragg peak at all: this is why visible light is not diffracted by crystals and why cold neutrons pass through a beryllium filter.

source.where: slide 23; no key on the slide, the answer is ours

questions.q: Yes or no? The larger the indices $hkl$, the larger the distance $d_{hkl}$.
questions.explain: The other way round: $d_{hkl}=2\pi/|\mathbf G_{hkl}|$, cubic $d=a/\sqrt{h^2+k^2+l^2}$. High indices are closely spaced planes and scatter to large angles.

source.where: slide 23; no key on the slide, the answer is ours

questions.q: Yes or no? Given a fixed wavelength $\lambda$, there is only a finite number of Bragg peaks.
questions.explain: $|\mathbf G|=\frac{4\pi}{\lambda}\sin\theta\le\frac{4\pi}{\lambda}$: only the reciprocal lattice points inside a sphere of radius $4\pi/\lambda$ can be reached (calculation fight "How many spots can the detector ever see?").

source.where: slide 23; no key on the slide, the answer is ours

questions.q: Yes or no? For a given pair $(\lambda,\theta)$ there can be at most a single Bragg peak.
questions.explain: $(\lambda,\theta)$ fixes only $d$. Several plane families can share one spacing: symmetry-equivalent ones such as $(100),(010),(001)$, or accidental ones such as $(300)$ and $(221)$ in a cubic crystal ($h^2+k^2+l^2=9$ for both). In a powder they fall on the same ring.

source.where: slide 23; no key on the slide, the answer is ours

questions.q: A neutron scattering experiment on a BCC lattice measures a Bragg peak at (100). What can we conclude?
options: The lattice consists of a single atomic species
The lattice consists of two atomic species
The lattice has an inversion symmetry
questions.explain: For identical atoms $F=f(1+e^{i\pi(h+k+l)})=0$ at $(100)$. With different scattering lengths on corner and centre, $F=f_1-f_2\ne0$: the peak appears, weakly (sheet 3 Q1c). The crystal is then really simple cubic with a two-atom basis (CsCl type, e.g. an ordered alloy).

source.where: slide 54; the slide marks this answer

questions.q: What scatters X-rays most strongly?
questions.explain: X-rays scatter off the electron charge density (Thomson scattering $\propto1/m^2$, so nuclei are negligible). Most electrons of an atom are core electrons, concentrated near the nucleus: the form factor $f(\mathbf q)$ grows with $Z$. Neutrons see the nuclei (and magnetic moments) instead.

source.where: slide 55; the slide marks this answer

questions.q: An X-ray beam on a cubic crystal powder gives a powder diffraction pattern. Which statement is <u>wrong</u>?
options: Rotating the sample changes the diffraction pattern
A ring can contain contributions from several lattice planes, such as (100), (010) and (001)
The pattern allows determining both the lattice type and the cell constant
For a given wavelength $\lambda$, several rings can appear
questions.explain: A powder contains crystallites in all orientations, so rotating it changes nothing: every $\mathbf G$ with $|\mathbf G|\le4\pi/\lambda$ is in reflection position for some grains and gives a ring (script 1.5.4). The ring radii give $d_{hkl}$, their sequence the lattice type (sheet 3 Q1).

source.where: slide 56; the slide marks this answer

questions.q: X-rays are directed at a single crystal with monoclinic symmetry. What happens?
options: The diffraction pattern changes as the crystal is rotated
For this crystal it is impossible to draw any conclusions on the structure from X-ray diffraction
With monochromatic X-rays the diffraction pattern shows rings
Each $hkl$ plane generates one Bragg peak
questions.explain: A single crystal has one orientation: a reflection appears only when $\mathbf k^\prime-\mathbf k=\mathbf G$ is met, so turning the crystal moves reciprocal lattice points through the Ewald sphere and the spots change. Rings need a powder. Low symmetry does not prevent structure determination.

source.where: slide 3; the slide marks this answer

questions.q: The powder pattern of sodium was measured at two temperatures $T_1$ (red, dotted) and $T_2$ (blue). The lattice expands on heating. Which statement is correct?
options: Sodium has a phase transition between $T_1$ and $T_2$
questions.explain: The $T_1$ peaks sit at larger $2\theta$. Bragg: $\sin\theta=\lambda/2d$, larger angle means smaller $d$, a smaller lattice constant, hence the colder sample: $T_1<T_2$. The same three peaks appear in both, so the structure (BCC: $h+k+l$ even) is unchanged.

source.where: slide 6; the slide marks this answer

questions.q: We measure several Bragg peaks $(hkl)$ with X-rays. Which concept describes their different intensities?
options: The size of the Brillouin zone
questions.explain: The lattice (Bragg or Laue condition) fixes where peaks can be; the basis fixes how strong they are: $I\propto|F(\mathbf G)|^2$, $F=\sum_jf_je^{i\mathbf G\cdot\mathbf r_j}$ (script 1.5.2, eq. 1.23).

source.where: slide 7; the slide marks this answer

questions.q: Which statement is <u>wrong</u>?
options: The symmetries of a crystal and of its diffraction pattern are identical
Diffraction peaks can only appear if the Bragg condition is fulfilled
The basis vector $\vec a^*$ of the reciprocal lattice is orthogonal to the basis vectors $\vec b$ and $\vec c$ of the direct lattice
The larger a crystal, the stronger the intensity of a Bragg peak
questions.explain: The pattern shows $I\propto|F(\mathbf G)|^2$ and $|F(-\mathbf G)|=|F(\mathbf G)|$ (Friedel): it always has inversion symmetry, even if the crystal has none, and the phases are lost (script 1.5.3). The other three hold: $\vec a^*\propto\vec b\times\vec c$, and the peak intensity grows with the number of cells.

source.where: slide 17; the slide marks this answer
Week 3 and the week-8 quiz (chapter 1.6): the concept questions asked in the lecture, with the answers marked on the slides

questions.q: $H=-\frac{\hbar^2\nabla^2}{2m}-\frac{e^2}{4\pi\epsilon_0r_A}-\frac{e^2}{4\pi\epsilon_0r_B}+\frac{e^2}{4\pi\epsilon_0R}$ describes the H$_2^+$ molecule (electron at distances $r_A,r_B$ from the nuclei A and B, which are $R$ apart). Which aspect is <u>neglected</u>?
options: Coulomb attraction between the electron and the nuclei
Electrostatic screening of the positive nuclear charges by the electron
questions.explain: There is no $-\frac{\hbar^2}{2M}\nabla_{A,B}^2$: the nuclei are treated as fixed at distance $R$ (Born–Oppenheimer: $M\gg m$). $R$ is a parameter, and the electronic energy $E(R)$ becomes the potential in which the nuclei move (script 1.6.4).

source.where: slide 32; the slide marks this answer

questions.q: Metallic bonding. Which statement is <u>wrong</u>?
options: The valence electrons can move freely between the atomic cores
The metallic bond has no preferential orientation
Metals are primarily FCC or HCP because this maximises the filling factor
All electrons are strongly localised at the atomic sites
questions.explain: The valence electrons are delocalised over the whole crystal: spreading out lowers their kinetic energy, and that gain is the bond (script 1.6.6). Only the core electrons stay localised. Because the bond is not directional, metals prefer close packing.

source.where: slide 33; the slide marks this answer

questions.q: List the solids in order of increasing cohesive energy per atom.
questions.explain: Van der Waals $<$ metallic $<$ ionic $<$ covalent: Ar $\approx0.08$, Na $\approx1.1$, NaCl $\approx3.3$, diamond $\approx7.4$ eV per atom (values from the slide; script Table 1.2 and 1.6.7).

source.where: slide 34; the slide marks this answer

questions.q: Which chemical bonding type is present in any material?
questions.explain: Fluctuating dipoles exist in every atom, so the $-1/r^6$ attraction is always there (script 1.6.1). It is usually hidden behind much stronger bonds and only decides the structure where nothing else acts: noble gases, between molecules, between graphene layers.

source.where: slide 5; the slide marks this answer

questions.q: Four configurations of atomic orbitals. Which do not lead to a covalent bond?
options: All configurations lead to covalent bonds
questions.explain: A bond needs a non-zero overlap (hopping) integral. In B and D the positive and negative lobes of one orbital overlap equally with the other orbital and the contributions cancel by symmetry. A (two parallel p: a $\pi$ bond) and C (d and p with matching lobe signs) have a net overlap.

source.where: slide 9; the slide marks this answer

questions.q: The H$_2^+$ molecule forms a bonding and an anti-bonding molecular orbital. Which statement is correct?
options: In the anti-bonding orbital the electron has a higher probability density between the nuclei than in the bonding orbital
The anti-bonding level has a lower energy than the bonding level
The wave function of the anti-bonding orbital is antisymmetric
The chemical bond of the H$_2^+$ molecule is called a hydrogen bond
questions.explain: Anti-bonding: $\psi_A-\psi_B$, antisymmetric with a node halfway, little charge between the nuclei, energy $E_0+t$. Bonding: $\psi_A+\psi_B$, charge piled up between the nuclei, energy $E_0-t$ (sheet 3 Q3). The bond is covalent; a hydrogen bond is something else (a proton shared between two electronegative atoms, script 1.6.5).

source.where: slide 10; the slide marks this answer

questions.q: Which orbitals are involved in the graphene carbon–carbon bonds?
questions.explain: Three sp$^2$ hybrids at 120° in the plane form the $\sigma$ bonds of the honeycomb; the remaining p$_z$ orbital forms the $\pi$ band, which gives the linear dispersion of sheet 6 Q2. sp$^3$ (four tetrahedral bonds) is diamond.

source.where: slide 15; the slide marks this answer
Week 4 and the week-8 quiz (chapter 2): the concept questions asked in the lecture, with the answers marked on the slides

questions.q: Normal modes of a simple cubic lattice with one atom per cell. Which statement about the wave vector $\vec q$ is correct?
options: Only this: $q$ can assume $N$ different values, $N$ being the number of unit cells
Only this: $q$ is confined to $(-\pi/a,\pi/a]$, $a$ being the lattice constant
Both: $q$ takes $N$ values, and they lie in $(-\pi/a,\pi/a]$
questions.explain: Periodic boundary conditions: $q=\frac{2\pi}{Na}p$, spacing $2\pi/L$. Values outside the first Brillouin zone repeat the same displacements, so exactly $N$ distinct $q$ remain (sheet 4 Q1b; script 2.2.4). The smallest positive one is $2\pi/L$, not $2\pi/a$.

source.where: slide 34; the slide marks this answer

questions.q: The Debye temperature is approximately proportional to ...
questions.explain: $k_BT_D=\hbar\omega_D=\hbar v_sk_D$ with $k_D=(6\pi^2n)^{1/3}$ fixed by the density of atoms. Stiff, light crystals (diamond: 2230 K) have a high sound velocity and a high $T_D$; soft, heavy ones (lead: 105 K) a low one.

source.where: slide 19; the slide marks this answer

questions.q: Silicon: two FCC lattices shifted by ¼ of the space diagonal. How many phonon branches are expected?
questions.explain: Count atoms in the primitive cell: 2 (the cube with 8 atoms is not primitive). $3\times2=6$ branches, always 3 acoustic, the remaining $3(p-1)=3$ optical (script 2.2.6).

source.where: slide 20; the slide marks this answer

questions.q: Which model is most suited to describe optical lattice modes?
questions.explain: Optical branches are nearly flat, $\omega(q)\approx\omega_E$: one frequency for all modes is exactly Einstein’s assumption (sheet 4 Q2). Debye ($\omega=v_sq$) describes the acoustic branches.

source.where: slide 21; the slide marks this answer

questions.q: Which phenomenon is <u>incompatible</u> with the harmonic approximation of lattice dynamics?
options: The specific heat approaches $C_V=3k_BN$ in the Dulong–Petit regime
questions.explain: In the harmonic crystal the normal modes are exact eigenstates: phonons never interact and live forever. Decay, thermal expansion and a finite thermal conductivity need the cubic and higher terms (script 2.3.3). Dulong–Petit is the harmonic result, and electron–electron interaction has nothing to do with it.

source.where: slide 22; the slide marks this answer

questions.q: Diatomic chain with masses $M_1$, $M_2$ and spring constant $f$ (the slides’ letter; the script calls it $k$, and writes the wave vector $q$). Which point 1–4 of the dispersion matches the mode shown (displacements drawn sideways)?
questions.explain: The two kinds of atoms move against each other (the open circles are displaced opposite to the filled ones): optical branch. The pattern repeats after $4a$: $k=\frac{2\pi}{4a}=\frac{\pi}{2a}$. Optical branch at $\pi/2a$ is point 3.

source.where: slide 23; the slide marks this answer

questions.q: Diatomic chain. Which assignment between the modes (1)–(4) and the points A–D of the dispersion is correct?
questions.explain: (Slide notation: $k$ is the wave vector, $f$ the spring constant; in the script $q$ and $k$.) D (acoustic, $k=0$): all atoms move together, a rigid shift: (1). A (optical, $k=0$): the two sublattices move against each other, identically in every cell: (2). At the zone boundary neighbouring cells are in antiphase and one sublattice stands still: in the optical mode B the light atoms move, $\omega^2=2f/M_{\rm light}$: (3); in the acoustic mode C the heavy atoms move, $\omega^2=2f/M_{\rm heavy}$: (4) (script 2.2.5).

source.where: slide 24; the slide marks this answer

questions.q: X-rays are inelastically scattered off a crystal. Upon scattering, the lattice vibrations change ...
questions.explain: Inelastic means a phonon $(\mathbf q,\omega)$ is created or absorbed: $\hbar\omega=E_i-E_f$, $\mathbf q=\mathbf k_i-\mathbf k_f+\mathbf G$ (script 2.3.2). One mode gains or loses a quantum: its amplitude changes, and with it which wavelengths and frequencies are present in the motion of the lattice.

source.where: slide 25; the slide marks this answer

questions.q: A lattice with optical and acoustic modes, two atom types with masses $M_1$ and $M_2>2M_1$. How can we increase the energy gap at the edge of the Brillouin zone?
options: By increasing the distance between atoms, leading to a weaker spring force
questions.explain: Notation of the slides: $f$ is the spring (force) constant between neighbours, $k$ the wave vector; the script writes the spring constant $k$ and the wave vector $q$. At the zone edge $\omega_{\rm opt}=\sqrt{2f/M_1}$, $\omega_{\rm ac}=\sqrt{2f/M_2}$ (light mass $M_1$ in the optical mode, heavy $M_2$ in the acoustic one). A heavier $M_2$ lowers the acoustic edge: the gap grows. A heavier $M_1$ lowers the optical edge: the gap shrinks. Doubling both, or weakening $f$, scales both frequencies down and the gap with them.

source.where: slide 26; the slide marks this answer

questions.q: Phonon dispersion of a one-dimensional chain. Which segment has the highest phonon density of states?
options: All segments have the same DoS
questions.explain: In 1D the $q$ values are equally spaced, so the number of modes per frequency interval is $g(\omega)\propto1/|d\omega/dq|$. Where the curve is flat (segment a, at the extremum) the most $q$ values fall into the same $\Delta\omega$: a van Hove singularity (script 2.4.2).

source.where: slide 27; the slide marks this answer

questions.q: Which of the following applies to optical modes of lattice vibrations?
options: Only this: they can be excited by electromagnetic waves
Only this: their frequency does not approach zero for $q\to0$, $\omega(q=0)\ne0$
Both: they can be excited by electromagnetic waves, and $\omega(q=0)\ne0$
questions.explain: $\omega(q\to0)\ne0$ is what defines an optical branch: the atoms of the basis move against each other. Coupling to light needs in addition that this motion carries an oscillating dipole, i.e. differently charged atoms (NaCl: yes; silicon or diamond: no). So "excited by light" is not true in general.

source.where: slide 28; the slide marks this answer

questions.q: Diatomic chain with masses $M>m$. What is the motion of the masses at point P (top branch, zone boundary)?
questions.explain: P is the optical branch at the zone boundary: $\omega^2=2f/m$, only the light masses move, and with $q=\pi/a$ neighbouring cells are in antiphase: pattern 4. Pattern 3 is the acoustic branch at the zone boundary, pattern 5 the optical mode at $q=0$, patterns 1 and 2 are not normal modes.

source.where: slide 29; the slide marks this answer

enc.title: Lecture questions: free electrons and specific heat

source.where: Week-8 quiz (chapter 3.1): the concept questions asked in the lecture, with the answers marked on the slides

questions.q: How does the specific heat of a free electron gas scale with temperature?
options: It depends on the temperature range
questions.explain: Only electrons within $\sim k_BT$ of $\epsilon_F$ can be excited: a fraction $T/T_F$, each gaining $\sim k_BT$. $C_{el}=\frac{\pi^2}{2}Nk_B\frac{T}{T_F}=\gamma T$ (script 3.1.4), valid for all $T\ll T_F$, i.e. for every solid metal.

source.where: slide 31; the slide marks this answer

questions.q: How does the specific heat of a phonon lattice scale with temperature?
options: It depends on the temperature range
questions.explain: $T\ll T_D$: $C\propto T^3$ (Debye). $T\gg T_D$: constant, $3Nk_B$ (Dulong–Petit). In between neither (script 2.4.3). So in a metal at low $T$: $C=\gamma T+\beta T^3$.

source.where: slide 32; the slide marks this answer

questions.q: What is the dominant contribution to the specific heat of a solid at room temperature?
questions.explain: Room temperature is of the order of $T_D$ for most solids, so all phonon branches are excited and give close to $3k_B$ per atom. The electrons add only $\sim\frac{\pi^2}{2}\frac{T}{T_F}k_B\approx1\%$ of that, because $T_F\sim5\times10^4$ K.

source.where: slide 33; the slide marks this answer

questions.q: An ideal electron gas in a box with $N_e$ electrons (neglect spin). How many electronic states does the crystal have?
options: More than $N_e$ states, but a finite number
questions.explain: Key of the slide. The occupied states are the $N_e$ lowest $\mathbf k$ points inside the Fermi sphere; more states lie above $\epsilon_F$ (otherwise nothing could be excited). In a real crystal the count is finite: each band holds $N$ values of $\mathbf k$ (one per unit cell), and there is one band per atomic orbital. For the idealised box alone one could argue "infinite" (no upper limit on $k$): if this comes up, ask how the lecturer wants it read.

source.where: slide 34; the slide marks this answer

questions.q: The wave functions of an ideal electron in a box are ...
options: plane waves (only a discrete number of $k$ allowed)
plane waves that obey the translational symmetry of the crystal
questions.explain: $\psi_{\mathbf k}=\frac{1}{\sqrt V}e^{i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf r}$ with periodic boundary conditions: $k_i=\frac{2\pi}{L}n_i$ (script 3.1.1). No lattice enters the free-electron model, so there is no crystal symmetry to obey; superpositions of plane waves (Bloch waves) only appear with a periodic potential.

source.where: slide 35; the slide marks this answer

questions.q: Which density of states $\nu(\epsilon)$ agrees best with the three-dimensional quasi-free electron model?
questions.explain: 3D free electrons: $\nu(\epsilon)\propto\sqrt\epsilon$ (script 3.1.2). Constant is 2D, $\propto1/\sqrt\epsilon$ is 1D (sheet 6 Q1).

source.where: slide 39; the slide marks this answer

questions.q: A "free-electron gas" ...
options: is best approximated by the tight-binding model
exhibits band gaps, that is, energies for which there are no electronic states
at $T=0$ has zero probability of having electrons with energies higher than the Fermi energy $\epsilon_F$
has an infinite number of energy bands
questions.explain: At $T=0$ the Fermi–Dirac distribution is a step: every state below $\epsilon_F$ full, every state above empty. Gaps and bands need a periodic potential; tight binding is the opposite limit (strongly bound electrons).

source.where: slide 47; the slide marks this answer

questions.q: What is a typical value for the Fermi temperature?
questions.explain: $\epsilon_F$ of a metal is a few eV (Na 3.2 eV, Cu 7 eV) and 1 eV corresponds to 11 600 K: $T_F\sim4$–$8\times10^4$ K. Hence the electron gas is degenerate at any temperature at which the metal is solid.

source.where: slide 48; the slide marks this answer

questions.q: Order the temperatures as they typically occur for metals: Fermi temperature $T_F$, Debye temperature $T_D$, melting point $T_S$.
questions.explain: $T_D\sim100$–$500$ K, $T_S\sim10^3$ K, $T_F\sim5\times10^4$ K. Example copper: 343 K, 1358 K, 81 600 K. Consequences: at room temperature the lattice is nearly classical, the electrons are deeply degenerate.

source.where: slide 49; the slide marks this answer

enc.title: Lecture questions: bands, Bloch, tight binding

source.where: Week-8 quiz (chapters 3.2–3.3): the concept questions asked in the lecture, with the answers marked on the slides

questions.q: In the nearly-free electron model a band gap is expected at the Brillouin zone boundary. As a consequence ...
options: this model can only be used to describe insulators
questions.explain: A gap alone decides nothing: what matters is where the Fermi level lies. A partly filled band gives a metal, completely filled bands an insulator or semiconductor (script 3.2.4). The same model describes both.

source.where: slide 36; the slide marks this answer

questions.q: A three-dimensional crystal with $N$ unit cells and $m$ atoms per unit cell; each atom has two valence electrons. How many discrete values are allowed for the electron wave vector $\vec k$?
questions.explain: The number of $\mathbf k$ values in the first Brillouin zone equals the number of unit cells, whatever sits in the cell (script 3.2.1). More atoms or electrons per cell mean more bands, not more $\mathbf k$ values. Each band then holds $2N$ electrons.

source.where: slide 37; the slide marks this answer

questions.q: Which band structure (1–4) matches the density of states shown at the top right?
questions.explain: Read the density of states as "how much band per energy slice": flat bands give peaks, steep bands little weight. The DoS has one smooth, low contribution from $-4$ to 0 eV (a single steep, free-electron-like band) and tall peaks between 0 and 4 eV (several flat bands crowded there). That is panel 1.

source.where: slide 38; the slide marks this answer

questions.q: Six sketched dispersion relations. Which one fits nearly-free electrons?
questions.explain: Nearly free: the free parabola $\hbar^2k^2/2m$ folded into the first zone, with gaps opened where the branches meet at the zone boundary (script 3.2.2). Key of the slide for the rest: tight binding 4 and 5 (cosine bands), phonons 1 (acoustic branch linear at small $k$ plus optical branch), Debye/Einstein approximation 6 (straight line plus constant), free electrons: none, and sketch 2 fits none of the models.

source.where: slide 40; the slide marks this answer

questions.q: Same six sketches. Which one shows phonons in the Debye / Einstein approximation?
questions.explain: Debye replaces the acoustic branch by the straight line $\omega=v_s|k|$, Einstein the optical branch by a constant $\omega_E$: sketch 6. Sketch 1 is the real diatomic chain (sine-like acoustic branch, weakly dispersing optical branch).

source.where: slide 40; the slide marks this answer

questions.q: The electronic density of states ...
options: is small at the zone boundary
is large at the zone boundary
becomes large at very high temperatures
questions.explain: At the zone boundary the bands flatten (zero slope, standing waves), so many $\mathbf k$ states share nearly the same energy: van Hove singularities. The density of states is a property of the band structure and does not depend on temperature.

source.where: slide 41; the slide marks this answer

questions.q: Nearly-free electrons in 1D, atoms at $x=na$. What is the approximate wave function at the boundary of the first Brillouin zone ($k_{BZ}=\pi/a$) in the lowest-energy configuration?
questions.explain: At the zone boundary $e^{i\pi x/a}$ and $e^{-i\pi x/a}$ are degenerate and mix into standing waves. $|\cos(\pi x/a)|^2$ piles the electron up on the ions at $x=na$, where the potential is attractive: lower energy. $\sin$ puts it between the ions: higher energy. The difference is the gap $2|U_G|$ (script 3.2.2).

source.where: slide 42; the slide marks this answer

questions.q: Nearly-free electrons, a BCC lattice with a one-atom basis, one valence electron per atom, $T=0$. Which statement is correct?
options: The material is an insulator, because the highest energy level is completely filled
If the highest electron bands overlap, the material is a metal; otherwise it is a semiconductor
The material is a metal, because the highest band cannot be completely filled
questions.explain: One atom per primitive cell and one electron per atom: $N$ electrons for a band that holds $2N$ (spin). The band is half full, the Fermi surface lies inside the first zone: a metal, no matter how large the gaps are. This is sodium (sheet 7 Q2).

source.where: slide 43; the slide marks this answer

questions.q: Which statement concerning the tight-binding model is correct?
options: Weakly bound electrons have narrower energy bands
Energy bands get wider with increasing overlap between atomic orbitals
The energies of the electrons are increased compared to the energies in the free atoms
questions.explain: Band width $=4t$ in 1D ($E=E_0-2t\cos ka$), and the hopping $t$ is the overlap matrix element between neighbouring orbitals (script 3.2.3, sheet 7 Q3). Weakly bound (extended) orbitals overlap more: wider bands. Bands from different orbitals can overlap.

source.where: slide 44; the slide marks this answer

questions.q: Pressure is applied to a simple cubic lattice: closer packing, same structure. In the tight-binding model, the energy bands ...
options: are raised in energy and become narrower
are raised in energy and become wider
are lowered in energy and become narrower
are lowered in energy and become wider
questions.explain: Closer atoms overlap more: $t$ grows, the band ($E_0\pm2t$ per direction) widens. The band centre drops too, because every orbital now feels more of its neighbours’ attractive potentials: in sheet 3 Q3, $E_0=\epsilon_0-V_0\kappa e^{-2\kappa d}$ falls as the distance $d$ shrinks.

source.where: slide 45; the slide marks this answer

questions.q: According to Bloch’s theorem, which equality is correct? ($\vec R$: direct lattice vector, $\vec G$: reciprocal lattice vector)
options: $\psi_{\vec k}(\vec r+\vec R)=\psi_{\vec k+\vec G}(\vec r)$
$\psi_{\vec k-\vec G}(\vec r)=e^{i\vec k\cdot\vec R}\psi_{\vec k}(\vec r)$
$\psi_{\vec k}(\vec r+\vec R)=e^{i\vec k\cdot\vec R}\psi_{\vec k+\vec G}(\vec r)$
questions.explain: Bloch: $\psi_{\vec k}(\vec r)=e^{i\vec k\cdot\vec r}u_{\vec k}(\vec r)$ with lattice-periodic $u$, so $\psi_{\vec k}(\vec r+\vec R)=e^{i\vec k\cdot\vec R}\psi_{\vec k}(\vec r)$: only a phase, not full periodicity. And $\vec k$ is defined up to $\vec G$: $\psi_{\vec k+\vec G}=\psi_{\vec k}$ (script 3.2.1). Together they give the marked option.
